title: Siquijor Island Marathon 2026 Review: A Second Race on the Island of Fires
meta_description: Siquijor Island Marathon 2026 review: September 26 -- a full marathon and shorter distances on Siquijor, weeks after the island's Isla del Fuego race.
dek: Set for 26 September 2026, this full marathon joins Isla del Fuego (covered elsewhere in this batch) as a second distinct race on Siquijor Island -- distances from 5K to 42.195K, roughly three weeks after the island's other September race.
verdict: The Siquijor Island Marathon is a distinct event from Isla del Fuego Marathon, held roughly three weeks apart on the same small island -- worth not confusing the two when planning travel. This one offers the full 42.195K distance alongside 21.1K, 10K and 5K, a step up from Isla del Fuego's own four-distance spread. Siquijor's genuine draw is its identity: nicknamed Isla de Fuegos by Spanish explorers for its fireflies, and historically associated (fairly or not) with folk healing and mysticism in Philippine popular culture. Registration status hasn't been announced yet, and organiser detail is thin.

sections.heading: A Second Race on the Same Small Island
paragraphs: The Siquijor Island Marathon offers 5K, 10K, 21.1K and the full 42.195K marathon. [1] This is a distinct event from the Isla del Fuego Marathon (also covered in this research, held 6 September 2026) -- both take place on Siquijor Island roughly three weeks apart, so runners planning a trip should be careful not to conflate the two when checking dates and registration.

sections.heading: The Island of Fires
paragraphs: Siquijor is a small island province in the central Visayas, in the Bohol Sea roughly 30km southeast of Negros. Early Spanish explorers called it Isla de Fuegos -- 'Island of Fires' -- for its swarms of fireflies; it became an independent province in 1971. [2] Beyond that colonial-era nickname, the island carries a distinct cultural identity in Philippine popular culture, often associated with folk healers and traditional mysticism -- a genuinely different destination character from most races in this research batch.

sections.heading: A Fuller Distance Spread
paragraphs: Unlike Isla del Fuego's four-category spread (5K/10K/21K/42K, matching this race's own distances), this marathon offers the same four categories -- meaning both Siquijor races give runners a full-marathon option, unusual for an island this size to support two separate marathon-distance events within a single month.

sections.heading: Thin Organiser Detail
paragraphs: Registration status for the Siquijor Island Marathon has not yet been announced, and available research material is limited to a single event-listing aggregator, with no named organiser confirmed. [1] That's less detail than is available for the island's other September race, Isla del Fuego, which at least has a confirmed NGO-linked organiser and some participant feedback.

sections.heading: Should You Run It?
paragraphs: If you're drawn to Siquijor's distinctive island identity and want a full-marathon option specifically, this race on 26 September 2026 is worth watching -- but confirm you're looking at the right event, since Isla del Fuego runs on the same island just weeks earlier. Wait for registration and organiser details to firm up before booking travel.

faqs.question: Is this the same race as Isla del Fuego Marathon?
faqs.answer: No -- they're distinct events held roughly three weeks apart on the same island (Isla del Fuego on 6 September, this marathon on 26 September 2026). Both offer 5K/10K/21K/42K distances, so double-check which one you're registering for. [1]

faqs.question: What distances are offered?
faqs.answer: Four: 5K, 10K, 21.1K, and the full 42.195K marathon. Registration status has not yet been announced, and available organiser detail is limited compared to some other Siquijor race listings. [1]

faqs.question: Why is Siquijor a distinctive race destination?
faqs.answer: Spanish explorers named it Isla de Fuegos ('Island of Fires') for its fireflies, and the island carries a distinct cultural identity in Philippine popular culture tied to folk healing traditions -- a genuinely different backdrop from most Southeast Asian race destinations. [2]
